aiProducts.title: PortfolioIQ
aiProducts.subtitle: A deployed Streamlit prototype demonstrating enterprise AI governance in action, running as a public demo on sample data.
aiProducts.summary: A deployed, 6-screen Streamlit prototype demonstrating a Centaur governance model for enterprise application portfolio rationalization. A deterministic, rules-based engine produces explainable recommendations; Claude powers a separate conversational analysis screen. Built to demonstrate enterprise AI product thinking beyond a simple chatbot, with governance, explainability, cost management, and human oversight built into the review workflow.
capabilities: Explainable rules-based recommendation engine: eight supporting signals displayed per application, some applied directly by the decision rules and others indirectly through the technical debt score

Jagged Frontier classification (a framework identifying where automated recommendations are reliable versus where human judgment is essential): Inside, Edge, or Outside, derived from a rules-based confidence score
Recommendation drift indicator (simulated in the prototype)
Conversational portfolio analysis powered by Claude, with the full portfolio supplied as context
Per-session API governance with call limits
Access-controlled AI features with a shared passphrase gate (no individual user accounts)
ServiceNow Table API connector with automatic CSV fallback (the public demo runs on sample CSV data)
artifacts: Public demo on Streamlit Community Cloud (sample data)
aiProducts.architectureNote: Design choices: recommendations come from deterministic rules, and Claude is used only for conversational analysis; context stuffing over a vector database at the current 15-application scale; direct Claude API calls over LangChain for transparency and control. The proposed roadmap outlines when each would change at scale.
businessValue: Demonstrates AI product thinking beyond output generation, with governance, explainability, and human oversight built into the review workflow
Includes a proposed 0→500 customer productization roadmap; its customer and revenue targets are hypothetical planning assumptions
Rapid end-to-end delivery demonstrates the ability to move quickly from concept to working software.
aiProducts.businessProblem: Enterprise application portfolios routinely include hundreds of systems, and retain, retire, or modernize decisions are often made on incomplete information or institutional memory rather than consistent, defensible criteria. Without structured decision support, organizations either move too slowly or make costly modernization mistakes.
aiProducts.productVision: The opportunity was to bring the same governance discipline used in the GE Vernova APM Dashboard to an AI-assisted version, one where automation accelerates the recommendation without removing human accountability for the decision.
aiProducts.technicalArchitecture: A governed decision-support architecture: enterprise portfolio data feeds a deterministic, rules-based scoring and recommendation layer; every recommendation is explainable and can be routed to a human review queue; and every decision is recorded in a session audit log with CSV export. Claude provides conversational analysis over the same data and does not set recommendations.
keyFeatures: Six-screen guided workflow from portfolio overview to a reviewed, exportable decision
Approve, override, or escalate recommendations in the review queue, with written rationale required for overrides
Session-level governance controls to manage API usage responsibly
Exportable decision audit log (CSV) for stakeholder and leadership review
aiProducts.blueprintConnection: PortfolioIQ demonstrates governance and executive decision support, with an illustrative, sample-data view of value tracking, the same disciplines the Blueprint treats as inseparable, applied here to AI-assisted portfolio decisions specifically.

aiProducts.title: AI Security Triage Dashboard
aiProducts.subtitle: Enterprise threat and vulnerability decision-support with human-in-the-loop governance.
aiProducts.summary: A governed AI decision-support demo that helps security analysts triage CVE vulnerabilities, phishing emails, and URL threat indicators. Built with the same governance pattern as PortfolioIQ: AI generates a triage summary and recommended action, the analyst decides, and every decision is recorded with its rationale. No security actions are automated.
capabilities: CISA KEV cross-reference -  live exploitation status overlaid on every CVE, separating theoretical severity from operational priority.
Live CVE feed from NIST NVD API with CVSS severity scoring and AI triage summaries

Phishing email analysis on a 10-email sample from a labeled public research corpus, demonstrating AI risk scoring, explainable recommendations, and triage workflow governance. A production version would need an email security gateway integration.
Static sample set of URL threat indicators with severity classification and AI-generated mitigation recommendations
Human-in-the-loop review queue: every recommendation requires an analyst decision, which is recorded
Override tracking - written rationale required before any AI recommendation is overridden
Full audit log across all three data sources with CSV export
Decision recording: AI recommends, the analyst decides, and every decision is logged (no automated actions)
artifacts: Public demo on Streamlit Community Cloud
aiProducts.architectureNote: Same governance pattern applied to a cybersecurity context: retrieve threat data from multiple sources, AI recommends, the analyst decides, and the audit log records every decision. Demonstrates pattern reusability across domains. Designed, built, and deployed in a few days.
businessValue: Addresses analyst triage consistency — AI surfaces relevant threat context so every analyst makes decisions from the same information baseline
Override counts show where analyst and AI judgment diverge
Demonstrates governance-first AI PM thinking applied to a new domain under time pressure
aiProducts.businessProblem: Security analysts face a constant volume of CVEs, phishing reports, and threat indicators, more than can be manually triaged with consistent judgment. Inconsistent triage means real threats get buried under noise, and different analysts reach different conclusions from the same data.
aiProducts.productVision: The opportunity was to apply the same governed AI pattern used in portfolio decisions to a different domain under real time pressure, testing whether the governance model generalizes rather than being specific to one use case.
aiProducts.technicalArchitecture: A shared governance pattern applied to security operations: threat data comes from live NVD and CISA KEV sources plus bundled phishing and URL sample data, AI generates a triage recommendation, the analyst decides, and every decision is captured in an audit trail.
keyFeatures: Unified triage view across CVEs, phishing reports, and URL threat indicators
Live exploitation status overlaid on every vulnerability, not just theoretical severity
Required written rationale before overriding any AI recommendation
Full exportable audit log across all three data sources
aiProducts.blueprintConnection: The Security Triage Dashboard demonstrates operational governance, the same human-in-the-loop, audit-first pattern used for portfolio decisions, applied to a different domain to test whether the governance model generalizes.

aiProducts.title: Semantic CMDB Search Tool
aiProducts.subtitle: Natural-language search across ServiceNow CMDB records
aiProducts.summary: A local prototype connecting to a ServiceNow Personal Developer Instance via REST APIs, generating embeddings with the OpenAI embeddings API, and storing them locally in ChromaDB for embedding-based semantic retrieval across CMDB test records.
capabilities: Live ServiceNow PDI connection via REST API
Highlights CMDB data quality impact on retrieval accuracy
artifacts: Working local prototype with end-to-end retrieval pipeline
businessValue: Intended: faster discovery of CMDB configuration records (not measured)
Intended: easier access to configuration details for non-specialists (not measured)
Demonstrates real-world constraints of CMDB data quality on AI retrieval
aiProducts.businessProblem: Enterprise CMDB systems hold critical information about system dependencies and infrastructure relationships, but keyword search fails when people don't know the exact naming conventions or system IDs, so valuable context routinely goes unfound.
aiProducts.productVision: The opportunity was to test whether natural-language search could make an existing CMDB investment more usable, without replacing or duplicating the system of record.
aiProducts.technicalArchitecture: A retrieval-based architecture: CMDB test records are embedded and indexed for semantic search, and natural-language queries return the most similar configuration records and their metadata rather than exact keyword matches.
keyFeatures: Natural-language query interface, no exact system names required
Returns the most similar configuration records with key metadata, beyond exact keyword matches
Connects to a ServiceNow developer instance via REST API
aiProducts.blueprintConnection: Semantic CMDB Search demonstrates organizational knowledge and AI-enabled discovery, making information the organization already has actually findable, one of the readiness gaps the Blueprint asks organizations to assess before scaling AI further.

aiProducts.title: Benefits Cost & Utilization Data Foundation
aiProducts.subtitle: Data foundation for benefits and claims analysis; AI capabilities planned
aiProducts.imageAlt: Benefits Cost & Utilization Data Foundation screenshot
aiProducts.summary: An early-stage data foundation for benefits and claims analysis: a local Bronze-layer Data Lakehouse with open datasets (CMS, BLS, Medicare) ingested and profiled. Predictive analytics, document intelligence, and conversational interfaces are planned and not yet built.
capabilities: Bronze-layer Data Lakehouse using CMS, BLS, and Medicare datasets
Datasets ingested and profiled for future cost and utilization analysis
Planned: predictive modeling and document intelligence
artifacts: Local data lakehouse with ingestion pipeline
businessValue: Intended: improved cost visibility for HR and finance stakeholders (hypothesis, not measured)
Roadmap shows path to conversational interface and HR system integration
aiProducts.businessProblem: HR and finance stakeholders need visibility into benefits cost and utilization trends, but the underlying data is often fragmented across sources and requires significant manual work to turn into a usable view.
aiProducts.productVision: The opportunity was to build an enterprise data architecture, from ingestion toward analytics, that could later support cost visibility and predictive, conversational capabilities as the roadmap matures.
aiProducts.technicalArchitecture: A layered data architecture: public benefits and claims data is ingested into a local lakehouse, providing the foundation for cost and utilization analysis and a path toward predictive and conversational capabilities.
keyFeatures: Public benefits datasets ingested and profiled
Structured, layered data pipeline designed for future growth
Roadmap toward predictive modeling and a conversational interface
aiProducts.blueprintConnection: The Benefits Analyzer demonstrates enterprise data architecture thinking, building the data foundation a capability needs before adding predictive or conversational features on top of it, the same sequencing discipline behind the Blueprint's Capability Gaps phase.

Consolidated quarterly view of 200+ applications for CIOs, directors, and application owners
Surfaced lifecycle and technical-debt risks to inform prioritization
enterpriseProjects.executiveSummary: Steam IT at GE Vernova needed a consolidated, actionable view of more than 200 applications to support investment decisions. I built a Smartsheet tracking and dashboard workflow, worked with application owners and technical teams to close governance gaps, and used it in quarterly reviews with CIOs, directors, and application owners.

sqdc.quality: Solution aligned with user needs through stakeholder-led requirements

outcomes: Migrated engineering documentation to the new SharePoint platform

Responded to early user feedback with week-long training
enterpriseProjects.executiveSummary: A retiring Lotus Notes knowledge system put access to years of engineering documentation at risk. This initiative replaced the platform and preserved access to the engineering knowledge it held.
enterpriseProjects.businessChallenge: The system was end-of-life, but it also held institutional knowledge accumulated over years, with no clean way to migrate it. Any misstep risked either losing critical documentation or disrupting engineering teams who had no tolerance for downtime.

Maintained stakeholder alignment throughout, communicating clearly on risks, decisions, and progress.
The second cutover completed with no reported post-launch data-integrity issues.

sqdc.safety: Mitigated operational and security risks from aging infrastructure
sqdc.quality: Migration validated before retry; no reported post-launch data-integrity issues
sqdc.delivery: Smooth, risk-managed rollout with proactive issue response

enterpriseProjects.challenge: Engineering's SharePoint 2007 environment had to be upgraded to a version supported by the data center.
outcomes: No reported post-launch data-integrity issues after the second cutover
Upgraded to a 64-bit version supported by the data center

enterpriseProjects.blueprintConnection: The decision to pause a live cutover rather than protect a deadline is the same judgment the Blueprint asks organizations to build into AI governance: knowing when to stop is as important as knowing how to scale.

hero.headline: From Enterprise Technology to Enterprise AI
narrative: Over ten years leading enterprise technology initiatives, I discovered that organizations rarely struggle because of technology alone. They struggle because governance, operating models, leadership, and adoption aren't connected. That realization ultimately led me to focus on how organizations operationalize Enterprise AI.
AI didn't introduce a new category of organizational failure. It exposed the same one, at a larger scale, moving faster, with less room to recover from getting it wrong.

leadership.label: ENTERPRISE LEADERSHIP
leadership.headline: Over ten years building the systems that determine whether technology investments actually work.
leadership.body: Product management, portfolio management, governance, decision support, and modernization, at executive scale, across GE Vernova, GE Power, Pratt & Whitney, and Alstom Power. That experience isn't the credential. It's the foundation the rest of this perspective is built on.

whyAI.label: WHY ENTERPRISE AI
whyAI.headline: The hardest problems were never really about the technology.
body: The deeper I got into enterprise technology leadership, the more I noticed that the hardest problems came down to whether an organization could govern a decision, build an operating model people would actually use, and get people to adopt a change instead of quietly working around it.

Enterprise AI didn't change that pattern. It raised the stakes on it. The organizations that succeed with AI won't be the ones with the best models, they'll be the ones who can operationalize it the way they'd operationalize any enterprise capability: with governance, ownership, adoption, and a way to measure whether it's actually working.

That's the problem I became interested in solving, not AI as a technology, but AI as something an organization has to be built to sustain. That interest is what eventually became the Enterprise AI Blueprint.

applied.label: BUILDING APPLIED AI
applied.headline: Testing the thinking by building it.
applied.body: My applied AI products demonstrate how these ideas translate into working software.

reflection.label: WHAT CHANGED
reflection.quote: Organizations rarely struggle because of the technology itself. They struggle because governance, operating models, product leadership, adoption, and business alignment were never connected to begin with, each one solved in isolation, if it gets solved at all. That realization became the foundation for everything I've built since.

lookingAhead.label: LOOKING AHEAD
lookingAhead.headline: Where I'm focused now.
lookingAhead.body: Helping organizations move from AI experimentation to a governed, scalable, measurable enterprise capability, the same disciplines that made a difference long before AI was the assignment, applied to the one in front of us now.

about.closing: Enterprise AI isn't just another technology shift. It's an organizational transformation. My work today is focused on helping organizations build the structures, governance, and leadership needed to make Enterprise AI a lasting business capability.
about.emotionalClose: Enterprise AI isn't the destination for me, it became the natural evolution of everything I'd spent my career solving. The technology changed. The organizational challenges did not.

pov.headline: My Point of View on Enterprise AI
pov.body: Most organizations are not failing at AI because of the models. They are struggling because they are applying AI to problems that have not been translated into clear, actionable decisions. AI does not solve problems directly. It supports decisions that address those problems. If the decision is not clearly defined, owned, and measurable, AI introduces risk instead of value.
pov.coreInsight: I view AI as a decision-support capability, not a decision-maker. The decision must be explicit, ownership must be assigned, and outcomes must be measurable and validated.
approach: Start with the decision: define what needs to be decided, who owns it, and what success looks like
Separate pattern work from judgment: AI supports pattern recognition, humans own tradeoffs
Keep AI in an advisory role with required human validation
Track false positives, false negatives, and business impact
Assign ownership and monitor outcomes through feedback loops

productApproach.title: Start with the Decision
productApproach.body: I define the decision we are trying to improve, who owns it, and what action it drives. If the decision is unclear, I do not move forward.

productApproach.title: Decompose the Workflow
productApproach.body: I map the end-to-end workflow, separating data retrieval, rules-based logic, pattern recognition, and human judgment to identify where AI actually fits.

productApproach.title: Choose the Right Approach
productApproach.body: I determine whether the problem requires rules, search, retrieval-based approaches, or machine learning. Not every problem needs AI.

productApproach.title: Design Human + AI Interaction
productApproach.body: I define what the AI does, what the human does, and where validation occurs. AI supports decisions, but humans remain accountable.

productApproach.title: Define Success & Risk
productApproach.body: I establish business metrics and assess risk early, ensuring outputs are measurable, reversible, and appropriate for the level of impact.

productApproach.title: Pilot, Measure, and Scale

hero.headline: Helping organizations operationalize Enterprise AI as a governed, scalable, and measurable business capability.
body: Most organizations can launch AI pilots. Far fewer can operationalize Enterprise AI across the business because operationalization requires more than technology. It requires governance, operating models, product leadership, adoption, and the organizational capabilities needed to sustain AI at enterprise scale.

Across more than ten years of enterprise technology leadership, including product strategy, governance, and application portfolio management at GE Vernova, I supported technology investment decisions for a portfolio of more than 200 applications.

Building on that experience, I developed the Enterprise AI Blueprint, a structured executive methodology that helps organizations assess AI readiness, identify capability gaps, design an operating model, and operationalize Enterprise AI responsibly and at scale.

pointOfView.label: POINT OF VIEW
pointOfView.headline: Enterprise AI is not simply a technology deployment. It is an organizational capability.
pointOfView.body: Organizations have become increasingly capable of funding AI pilots and deploying new tools. Far fewer establish the enterprise capabilities required to consistently select the right initiatives, govern them responsibly, coordinate delivery, drive adoption, and measure sustained business value.
pointOfView.pullQuote: AI becomes an enterprise capability when governance, delivery, adoption, and value realization operate as one system.

blueprint.label: STRUCTURED METHODOLOGY
blueprint.headline: The Enterprise AI Blueprint
body: The Enterprise AI Blueprint is a structured executive methodology I developed to help organizations understand their current position, assess readiness, identify capability gaps, establish an operating model, operationalize AI, and connect implementation to measurable business outcomes.

It draws on more than ten years of enterprise technology leadership, recent applied AI product work, and focused research into how organizations move AI from experimentation to sustained enterprise capability.

steps.title: Current State
steps.body: Understand where the organization stands today.
steps.question: Where does our organization actually stand today, beyond isolated pilots?
steps.purpose: Establish an honest, evidence-based picture of existing AI activity, technology investment, and organizational capability before committing to a path forward.
steps.outcome: A shared, factual understanding of current-state reality that leadership can act on with confidence.

steps.title: AI Readiness
steps.body: Assess organizational readiness to adopt AI responsibly.

steps.purpose: Evaluate whether the governance, talent, data, and operational foundations exist to support AI initiatives at the level leadership intends to pursue them.
steps.outcome: A readiness position that keeps the organization from scaling AI faster than it can govern.

steps.title: Capability Gaps

steps.question: What actually stands between where we are and where we need to be?
steps.purpose: Identify the organizational, technical, and governance gaps that will determine whether AI initiatives succeed or stall.
steps.outcome: A prioritized view of what must be built, acquired, or strengthened before scaling.

steps.title: Operating Model

steps.question: Who owns AI decisions, and how do initiatives actually get governed and delivered?
steps.purpose: Define the structure, accountability, and decision rights required to move AI from ad hoc activity to a managed enterprise function.
steps.outcome: A defined operating model that gives leadership a repeatable way to govern and deliver AI initiatives.

steps.title: Operationalize AI

steps.question: How do we move from a successful pilot to a capability the business actually relies on?
steps.purpose: Translate the operating model into practice, connecting delivery, adoption, and change enablement so AI becomes part of how the organization works.
steps.outcome: AI capability that is adopted, trusted, and embedded in real business workflows.

steps.question: How do we know this is actually working, and how do we sustain it?
steps.purpose: Connect implementation back to measurable business value, establishing the feedback loops that justify continued investment.
steps.outcome: A defensible, measurable link between AI investment and business results.

hero.headline: The Enterprise AI Blueprint
body: The Enterprise AI Blueprint is a structured executive framework for moving Enterprise AI from isolated pilots to a governed, scalable, and measurable business capability.

The Enterprise AI Blueprint emerged from a simple observation: the organizational disciplines that determine whether enterprise technology succeeds also determine whether Enterprise AI succeeds. Governance, product leadership, operating models, adoption, and value realization are not AI-specific. They are enterprise capabilities that become even more critical as organizations operationalize AI.
That perspective was shaped through more than ten years leading enterprise technology investment, governance, and product management at GE Vernova, GE Power, Pratt & Whitney, and Alstom Power.

struggle.label: WHY ORGANIZATIONS STRUGGLE
struggle.headline: Launching an AI pilot is often the easy part. Building the governance, operating model, and organizational capabilities required to sustain AI as an enterprise capability is much harder.
struggle.intro: Pilots are relatively easy to fund and easy to demo. What's difficult is everything after the demo: governance that holds up under real use, delivery that survives contact with existing systems, adoption that outlasts the initial enthusiasm, and a way to prove the investment was worth it. Most AI initiatives don't fail because the model was wrong. They stall because the organization never built the capability to run them at scale.

patterns.title: Treated as a project, not a capability
patterns.body: The pilot succeeds, then ends, because there was never a plan to operate it as an ongoing part of the business.

patterns.title: Governance added after the fact
patterns.body: Oversight gets bolted on once something goes wrong, instead of being designed into the initiative from the start.

patterns.title: Adoption left to chance
patterns.body: The tool is deployed, but no one owns whether people actually change how they work because of it.

steps.label: THE SIX-STEP BLUEPRINT
steps.headline: A structured path from fragmented activity to operational AI capability.
steps.intro: Each phase answers a specific executive question. Together, they move an organization from uncertainty about where it stands to a governed capability it can measure and sustain.

howItWorks.label: HOW THE BLUEPRINT WORKS
howItWorks.headline: Each phase builds on the one before it.
body: The Blueprint is sequential, not because process demands it, but because each phase produces something the next phase depends on. You cannot design a credible operating model before you understand your actual readiness. You cannot operationalize AI at scale on top of a governance structure that doesn't yet exist.

In practice, the phases are iterative. Organizations revisit earlier phases as conditions change, new initiatives emerge, or readiness gaps close. What stays constant is the discipline of not skipping ahead. Most of the AI initiatives that stall did so because a later-stage problem, usually adoption or governance, was never addressed at the stage where it needed to be.

relationship.label: RELATIONSHIP TO ENTERPRISE AI
relationship.headline: The Blueprint connects the disciplines that operationalizing AI actually requires.
relationship.body: Enterprise AI is not one initiative or one technology decision. It is the product of several disciplines operating as a single system, and the Blueprint is the structure that connects them.

closing.headline: Ready to operationalize Enterprise AI?
closing.body: The Blueprint is the framework. The conversation is where it gets specific to your organization's current state, constraints, and goals.

principles.label: PRODUCT THINKING
principles.headline: Five principles behind how these get built.

items.title: Start With the Decision
items.body: Define what needs to be decided, who owns it, and what success looks like before any model gets involved.

items.title: Separate Pattern From Judgment
items.body: AI supports pattern recognition. Humans own the tradeoffs and the accountability.

items.title: Keep AI Advisory
items.body: Every recommendation requires human validation before it becomes an action.

items.title: Track What Goes Wrong
items.body: False positives, false negatives, and business impact should be measured, not assumed. The current prototypes record analyst overrides; formal error measurement is planned.

items.title: Assign Ownership
items.body: Every capability has a named owner and a feedback loop that keeps it honest over time.
